routes.label: Cross one level at a time

question:
A frog hops along the number line according to the following rules. It starts at \(0.\) If it is at \(0,\) then it moves to \(1\) with probability \(\tfrac12\) and it disappears with probability \(\tfrac12.\) For \(n = 1,\) \(2,\) or \(3,\) if it is at \(n,\) then it moves to \(n + 1\) with probability \(\tfrac14,\) it moves to \(n - 1\) with probability \(\tfrac14,\) and it disappears with probability \(\tfrac12.\)

What is the probability that the frog reaches \(4?\)
solution:
Returning to a position gives the frog the same future chances as before. We can therefore describe its eventual success probability using only its current position.

Let \(p_n\) be the probability of eventually reaching 4 when starting at \(n\). We have \(p_4=1\). Starting at 0, the frog must first survive and move to 1, so
\[
p_0=\frac12p_1.
\]
For \(n=1,2,3\), split according to the first hop. A right hop contributes \(\frac14p_{n+1}\), a left hop contributes \(\frac14p_{n-1}\), and disappearing contributes zero. Thus
\[
p_n=\frac14p_{n-1}+\frac14p_{n+1},
\]
which rearranges to
\[
p_{n+1}=4p_n-p_{n-1}.
\]
Set \(p_0=x\). The equation at 0 gives \(p_1=2x\). Now compute successively:
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_2&=4(2x)-x=7x,\\
p_3&=4(7x)-2x=26x,\\
p_4&=4(26x)-7x=97x.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(p_4=1\), we obtain \(97x=1\). The frog starts at 0, so the requested probability is
\[
p_0=\boxed{\frac1{97}},
\]
choice \(\text{E}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
Every successful journey must reach 1, then 2, then 3, then 4. We can multiply the probabilities of completing these successive stages, allowing any number of backward excursions during each stage.

Let \(q_n\) be the probability that a frog starting at \(n\) reaches \(n+1\) before disappearing. At 0 there is only one way to make progress, so \(q_0=\frac12\).

Consider a stage starting at \(n=1,2,\) or \(3\). The frog can hop directly right, with probability \(\frac14\). Alternatively, it can hop left and eventually return to \(n\). The probability of that complete left-and-return excursion is
\[
r=\frac14q_{n-1}.
\]
After returning, it has exactly the same chances as when the stage began, because the rules depend only on its position.

A successful stage consists of some number \(k\ge0\) of these excursions followed by a right hop. Its probability is \(r^k\cdot\frac14\). The number of excursions is uniquely determined by the path, so these cases are disjoint and include every successful path. Therefore
\[
q_n=\frac14(1+r+r^2+\cdots).
\]
Since \(0\le q_{n-1}\le1\), we have \(0\le r\le\frac14<1\). The geometric series consequently sums to \(1/(1-r)\), giving
\[
q_n=\frac{1/4}{1-q_{n-1}/4}=\frac1{4-q_{n-1}}.
\]
Starting with \(q_0=\frac12\), this yields
\[
q_1=\frac1{4-1/2}=\frac27,\qquad
q_2=\frac1{4-2/7}=\frac7{26},\qquad
q_3=\frac1{4-7/26}=\frac{26}{97}.
\]
Upon first reaching each new position, the next stage has its corresponding probability \(q_n\), regardless of the earlier path. By multiplying these successive conditional probabilities, the chance of reaching 4 from 0 is
\[
q_0q_1q_2q_3
=\frac12\cdot\frac27\cdot\frac7{26}\cdot\frac{26}{97}
=\boxed{\frac1{97}},
\]
choice \(\text{E}\).
